title: RESP Basics
subtitle: Nowhere else in personal finance can you put in a dollar and have the government hand you back twenty cents, guaranteed.

blocks.text: Nowhere else in personal finance can you put in a dollar and have the government add twenty cents, guaranteed, with no market risk.

That’s what happens with an RESP, a Registered Education Savings Plan, when you save for a child’s education after high school. Yet many eligible families never claim it, because nobody explained how the matching works.
This lesson fixes that.
Collect every dollar of free education money your child is entitled to.
blocks.detail: A few well-timed deposits can add thousands in government grants to your child’s school fund.
blocks.extra: Section 03 shows the deposit that earns the full grant each year.

sections.title: The basic shape of an RESP

blocks.text: An RESP is an account you open for a child, usually as a parent or grandparent. You put money in. It grows inside the account, sheltered from tax. And the government adds money on top, through a grant called the CESG.

When the child goes to college, university or a trade program, the money comes out to help pay for it. The growth and grants are then taxed in the student’s hands, and most students pay little or no tax.
Unlike an RRSP, contributions aren’t tax-deductible. But growth inside the account is sheltered, and the grants are where the real value is.

sections.title: The CESG: the twenty cents on every dollar

blocks.text: The Canada Education Savings Grant matches 20% of what you put in, up to a limit.
Put in $2,500 in a year, and the government adds $500. That’s the sweet spot: the most grant a normal year can earn.
There’s a lifetime cap too. Once a child has received $7,200 in CESG, the grant stops, however much more you put in.
RESP grant numbers

items.title: Grant match
items.text: 20% — on the first $2,500 you put in each year.

items.title: Full yearly grant
Lifetime grant cap
items.text: $7,200 — after that, deposits earn no more grant.

items.title: Lifetime deposit limit
items.text: $50,000 — the most anyone can put in for one child.

items.title: “Contributing a big lump sum early gets you more grant money faster.”
items.text: It’s the opposite. The CESG only matches the first $2,500 put in each year. Deposit $15,000 in one year, and you still earn $500 in grant that year. The other $12,500 earns no grant. Spreading deposits over the years is how you collect the full $7,200.

blocks.text: CREDIT PULSE SPOTLIGHT: THE EXTRA GRANT LAYERED ON TOP OF THE 20%

The base 20% isn’t the whole match for every family. Households below certain income limits get the Additional CESG: an extra 10% or 20%, but only on the first $500 put in each year. For a lower-income family, that lifts the match on that first $500 to 30% or 40%. It doesn’t change the $7,200 lifetime cap, but it makes the first $500 each year worth more. Your RESP provider applies it based on your family income, so ask about it when you open the account.

Don’t wait until the teen years. The grant stops at the end of the year the child turns 17. A child aged 16 or 17 only qualifies if at least $2,000 was put in before they turned 16, or at least $100 a year in any four years before then. Starting early keeps the door open.

sections.title: Behind on contributions? There’s a catch-up rule

blocks.text: Missed a few years, or started late? The unused grant room doesn’t vanish.
It carries forward. You can catch up by putting in up to $5,000 in one year, which earns up to $1,000 in grant instead of the usual $500: one year of current room plus one year carried forward.
You can’t catch up faster than that, even with years of room built up. The most grant any single year can earn is $1,000.
CREDIT PULSE SPOTLIGHT: FREE MONEY WITH NO CONTRIBUTION REQUIRED

There’s a second payment worth knowing about, and it needs nothing from you except opening the account. The Canada Learning Bond is for lower-income families, and it pays into an RESP with no deposit required. For each eligible child born in 2004 or later, it pays $500 the first year and $100 for each later year the family qualifies, up to $2,000 by age 15. Families sometimes think an RESP is only worth opening if they can save regularly. For a lower-income household, opening the account alone can be worth real money. Young adults aged 18 to 20 who missed out can apply for themselves.

sections.title: What happens if the child doesn’t pursue further education

blocks.text: This question stops some families from opening an RESP at all, so it’s worth a clear answer.
Your own deposits always come back to you, tax-free, whatever happens. That part is never at risk.

The government money is different. If the child doesn’t go on to a qualifying program, the grants and bonds go back to the government. The growth can move into your own RRSP, up to $50,000, if you have the room and the plan meets the conditions. Otherwise it is taxed as your income, plus an extra 20% tax.

In practice, RESPs are flexible. Qualifying programs include university, college, trade school and apprenticeships, full-time or part-time. A family plan can also be shared among siblings, and you can keep the plan open for many years in case a child starts school later. The all-or-nothing fear is usually bigger than the real risk.

items.title: “If my child doesn’t go to university, I lose everything I put into the RESP.”
items.text: Your own deposits come back to you either way, tax-free. Only the government money needs repaying if the child never takes a qualifying program, and “qualifying” covers far more than a four-year degree, including trades and apprenticeships.

sections.title: Getting the most from an RESP

items.title: I’ve opened an RESP for my child, even if I can only contribute a small amount right now.
I’m putting in close to $2,500 a year, if I can, to collect the full yearly grant.
I know whether my family’s income qualifies for the Canada Learning Bond, which needs no deposit.
If I’m behind on contributions, I know the catch-up rule and its $1,000-per-year cap.
I’m not assuming one big deposit earns more grant than spreading it out. It doesn’t.

sections.title: The Okafor family’s first RESP year

blocks.text: The Okafor family’s first RESP year
paragraphs: When their daughter Ada was born in Calgary, the Okafors got a surprise gift from her great-aunt: $6,000, labelled in shaky handwriting “for the baby’s future.” Their first thought was to open an RESP and drop it all in at once, then cross it off the list.

At the bank, the adviser asked one question before they signed: how much would they be able to add in the next few years? Chidi and Grace looked at each other. With daycare costs coming, the honest answer was “not much.”

She showed them the grant math. All $6,000 in this year would earn $500 in grant, the most one year allows. The rest would still grow, but it would earn no grant, and with money tight, they might never catch up later.

They had a choice. Putting it all in now meant more time for the money to grow. Spreading it out meant more free grant money. They chose to spread it: $2,500 this year, $2,500 next year and $1,000 the year after, keeping the rest in a savings account until then.

That plan earned $1,200 in grants instead of $500. Then the adviser added a twist they hadn’t expected. Because their family income was below the limit, the first $500 they put in each year also earned the Additional CESG, a little extra on top.
Grace taped the great-aunt’s note inside Ada’s baby book. Under it, she wrote the three deposit dates, so “the baby’s future” would get every dollar it was owed.

blocks.text: The CESG matches 20% of RESP deposits, up to $500 a year and $7,200 per child, but only on the first $2,500 each year, so spreading deposits out earns more grant than one big deposit. Lower-income families may also get the Canada Learning Bond with no deposit at all. And your own deposits are never at risk, even if your child’s path changes.
A simple deposit schedule can turn one gift into far more for your child’s education.
blocks.detail: Spacing your deposits to match the grant rules collects the free money each year and keeps your own savings safe.

items.text: Money for lower-income families’ RESPs, paid with no deposit required.

items.title: Subscriber
items.text: The person who opens the RESP and puts money in, usually a parent or grandparent.

items.text: The child the RESP is set up for.

items.text: An eligible program after high school, including university, college, trade school and apprenticeships.
